doc.title: Kenny Davern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001 [interview 2 of 2]

title: White revivalists, black musicians and the problem with tribute shows
summary: He rejects claims that white musicians appropriated the music, praises older black mentors, and says tributes force players into repertory.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I’m curious as to why in this style of music that’s played at these festivals and parties, there’s very few younger black musicians playing it. Do you have any thoughts on that?

Well it wasn’t really hip for them to want to know this kind of music. I mean period. I mean they claim we appropriated the music, we white folks appropriated their music. Which is a lot of shit. Because if it wasn’t for the white guys who played this kind of music, that music would have died probably after 1930 you know, when blacks threw up the music or gave it up. And they went on to listening to swing or whatever. And a lot of the blacks that I played with who were encouraging to me, Dickie Wells, Rex Stewart, Claude Hopkins, Herman Autrey, numbers and numbers of guys who are all gone now unfortunately, they were the masses. Red Allen, you know Buck Clayton. These were the guys who said, who were helpful and encouraging. You play this music. Along comes this young guy and he says that he’s going to show everybody how it’s supposed to be done all over again. And some 40 years after the fact. And he doesn’t do a good job of it, we find it actually in his hands, and we know who we’re talking about. The music has not really been absorbed. It’s not his, he hasn’t really dined with the people that he’s supposedly or purportedly supposedly listened to and digested etc. He really hasn’t dined with them at all. Maybe he had a crust of bread with them. But he really hasn’t spent, really devouring the people that he proclaims to have — well he’s going to show everybody how it’s supposed to be. Well not in my book. It’s crap. And we who really believe the music have been just sort of like pushed out of the scene. Period. Fine. You know, I resent it but I don’t give a shit. I’m old enough to know what I do and ain’t nobody out there that does what I do, and there may be somebody out there that doesn’t do what I do but does what he does as good as me or maybe not as good as me, or better than me. But he ain’t going to do what I do. So that’s why this whole thing about all these tributes and all this kind of stuff, a tribute to — I really despise that. I think that that’s a crock. They won’t let you be who you are. They want you to hide behind somebody else and make them the reason why you’re all coming to this party to hear — the music of Fats Waller or this week Bix Beiderbecke will be our — next week, oh it’s going to be Louis Armstrong. Oh the Kid Ory night is Thursday. Oh really? And really, all of a sudden, how are you going to get individual voices if you are forcing people into

repertory. Where you’re really making them sound like somebody else other than themselves. Not that everybody wants to be themselves, because a lot of people don’t have self. You know they’re comfortable being other people or putting a different hat on.
Yeah. Certain people have made almost a career out of being close.
Well you’re a guy who I can always count on for an opinion.
Yeah well I’m sure I’ve rambled on much more than you ever wanted me to ramble on.
